items.content:
【Tianfeng Securities Overseas Tech】 After reviewing all the various AI related earnings, we believe the AI bull market is returning on the back of strong fundamentals

One very clear trend is emerging from the recent earnings of companies across the AI industry chain. Growth in cloud businesses is accelerating again, and compute demand continues to exceed supply. Customers are showing a willingness to accept price increases and even to prepay, and the unit economics of AI infrastructure are improving. Market attention is shifting away from concerns about excessive capital expenditure (CapEx) and back toward the belief that demand and profitability will actually materialize.

Large cloud: The slope of cloud business growth turned upward this quarter, and the scale of new bookings in the quarter was overwhelmingly larger than in any of the past 20 quarters.

Google has effectively no choice but to go all in. The mindset is that failure means the end. Even with negative free cash flow (FCF), every $1 of incremental cloud revenue converts into roughly $0.54 of new operating profit. On a simple calculation, the payback period is about 2 years.

AWS's margin of 39.4% is very strong. This provides an answer to the questions about return on investment (ROI). AWS will ultimately become a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue, with roughly 5x of growth headroom over the long term. The payback period for the cloud business is also under 3 years.

Microsoft: Azure's growth reaccelerated, providing an answer to concerns about the durability of that growth.

Neocloud: Earnings, demand, pricing power, and financing capability have all been validated across the board.

CoreWeave's (CRWV) recent compute resources are effectively all sold, with multiple customers competing to secure GPU volume. It added about 500MW of active power in a single quarter, and its year end target has been raised to more than 1.85GW. Its customer base is also broadening from large AI model companies and cloud giants to industrial, financial, life sciences, government, and traditional enterprises. AI is moving from a training centered frenzy toward a phase of adoption across every industry.

CoreWeave raised prices across all SKUs by about 25% in July. The profit contribution rate on new contracts rose by 5 to 10 percentage points. This shows that customers judge the returns they earn from AI to be sufficient to absorb higher compute prices. Even the A100, launched in 2020, is being signed into high priced contracts running through 2029. This also refutes the core bear case that GPUs are rapidly rendered obsolete within 3 to 4 years and that their residual value goes to zero.

Nebius (NBIS) saw total new contract value in the second quarter grow roughly 4x versus the prior quarter, with new customer contracts up more than 9x. Price tolerance on the demand side is so strong that, under current terms, it could sell all of its 2027 capacity today.

Annual revenue on new contracts reaches $20 million to $25 million per MW. Pricing on prior generation GPUs also rose more than 30% versus the prior quarter, and short term total bookings reach as much as $40 million to $50 million per MW. Customers have begun prepaying the cost of building AI infrastructure. About 70% of new contracts include prepayment provisions, which can cover 50% to 60% of the related CapEx. Expected project payback periods have shortened from 2 to 3 years previously to 1 year and 10 months. This means AI infrastructure is not simply a business that scales while burning cash, but one that has already secured strong unit economics.

Optical communications: The FCC related disruption is limited and the practical impact should be minimal. Lumentum (LITE) reported results above market expectations and raised guidance. EML demand exceeds supply by about 30%. The shortage of ultra high power lasers also continues to widen. Innolight's laser products are effectively sold out, and it plans to expand capacity roughly 4x over the coming quarters. The bottleneck remains delivery capability.

Quarterly OCS revenue clearly exceeded $100 million for the first time. NPO is not a technology that replaces CPO but a newly added intermediate architecture. Key customers' CPO plans are unchanged and demand signals are getting stronger. AI architecture is becoming increasingly optically integrated.

Memory and storage: It is now nearly certain that a bottom is forming. The core logic is to take time to secure room for recovery. The absence of price increases after the share price decline is already reflected in market expectations, and visibility on long term agreements (LTA) and shareholder returns is steadily improving.

Compute: The market narrative is shifting back toward AI training and open source. We are positive that Nvidia (NV) will challenge its prior high, and a narrative around RSI is also gradually forming.

👀Jeff Pu (@sssjeffpu)Monthly Wrap-Up of Aug Edition

* Tech index Moving from "unwind & consolidation" toward a "longer rebound" as August and 3Q26 begin.
* The worst of the pullback may be behind us due to SOX valuations correcting to 27x forward P/E, cleaned-up positioning, and better sentiment.
* The rebound could be longer than expected considering most expect it to be short lived. 
* Sector trends are uneven, with some AI semis appearing past peak, while our preferences remain for GPU/CPU/Optics.
* Reit CSP Capex Forecast: U.S. CSP capex is forecasted at +85% YoY in 2026 and +45% YoY in 2027.
* Reit CSP debt issuance is expected to be $257bn in 2026 and $419bn in 2027, leaving balance sheets very healthy with net leverage at 0.5 and net debt-to-equity at 18% by 2029.
* Reit U.S. CSP capex is projected to grow +20% YoY in 2028 (at the higher end of consensus), representing a deceleration as focus shifts to returns and LLM competition risks.
* Neoclouds continue to show robust spending.
* Earnings & Foundry: Leading foundry TSMC shows a solid outlook, alongside mature nodes, ASE, SPE, optics, CPU/ABF, and PMICs.
* Muted Near-Term: Near-term outlook is muted for smartphones (QCOM, AAPL, Xiaomi) and copper foil
* NAND & Anthropic: Third-party research indicates emerging NAND oversupply in 2H27 (consistent with our cautious view) and Anthropic ARR reached roughly $73bn by mid-July.
* Reit NVDA content shift from memories to optics, leading to higher adoption of NVL576 in 2027. NPO OE to benefit SMTC, MRVL
* CPO Expectations Already reset; hence, the ramp of scale out CPO in 4Q (could be stronger than expected) and NPO to be catalysts to LITE, COHR, GLW, Browave

items.content:
According to Taiwanese media reports, Nvidia plans to launch an 800VDC power rack compatible with the MGX architecture in the second half of 2026.

The product can be integrated directly into existing AC infrastructure and delivers 800VDC power to compute racks within the same rack row. Since it does not require major retrofitting of existing buildings and power supply systems, it is expected to lower the upgrade threshold for existing AI data centers.

Nvidia also plans to go a step further and introduce a "Row Power Center" for newly built or high density AI factories. This approach feeds power to multiple rack rows through an overhead 800VDC busway, supports up to 2MW per rack row, and is set to enter actual deployment from 2027. Over the longer term, Nvidia intends to adopt a "DC Power Block" that converts grid electricity directly into 800VDC at the facility level, building out a power delivery architecture for AI factories aimed at the next decade.

items.title: > > Silicon Wafer Prices Officially Raised According to Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), two leading silicon wafer producers have resumed price quotations one after another. The latest prices are 0.9 yuan per piece for the 183mm N-type wafer, 1.0 yuan per piece for the 210R N-type wafer, and 1.1 yuan per piece for the 210mm N-type wafer. These wafer prices are 0.1 yuan per piece higher than before. SMM assessed that the increase is closely tied to cost related policy. Wafer producers' actual raw material procurement costs have risen, lifting input costs along with them, so the price increase is a natural result, according to SMM.

items.content:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics Flashes Red on Glass Substrate Customer Evaluation... Investment Pushed Back Too

Samsung Electro-Mechanics' investment schedule for semiconductor glass substrates is slipping. A bottleneck has emerged in the customer's prototype reliability evaluation.

As a result, the timeline for building out the production line at GlaSSEM, the glass core joint venture, has also been pushed back, and the timing of related equipment orders has become murky.

According to multiple industry officials on the 12th, GlaSSEM, the glass core joint venture between Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Dongwoo Fine-Chem, has been unable to give its partners an equipment order schedule. One industry official said, "As recently as the end of July the mood was that orders were imminent, but right now it is hard to predict when they will resume," adding, "The schedule has been postponed several times, so at this point it has become difficult even internally to roughly estimate when orders will be placed."

Samsung Electro-Mechanics had been conveying equipment orders to partners for the GlaSSEM production line since November last year, but the schedule was pushed back at least three times, to December last year, then March, then June this year. After June, guidance on any follow up schedule disappeared altogether.

The industry points to the failure to obtain reliability evaluation certification for the glass substrate prototype from a global communications chip customer. A person familiar with the matter said, "I understand that the investment schedule was halted because Samsung Electro-Mechanics failed to pass the reliability evaluation," and "Since the prototype has to be remade and resubmitted, further delays to the existing schedule are unavoidable." The person added, "Because a new prototype cannot be produced within one or two weeks, whether the line investment happens within this year is also uncertain."

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is currently making glass substrate prototypes at its Sejong campus. To move to initial volume production, the step after pilot production, it is preparing to build a production line at GlaSSEM, the joint venture with Dongwoo Fine-Chem, a subsidiary of Japan's Sumitomo Chemical. Selection of the main process equipment suppliers, covering deposition, etching, laser drilling and inspection, is mostly complete.

Last month, expectations ran high among equipment makers that orders would begin in August. Samsung Electro-Mechanics had planned to start with deposition tools, which carry the longest lead times, bring the main process equipment into Dongwoo Fine-Chem's Pyeongtaek campus and install it by April next year, and complete the initial production line within the second quarter. It is also known to have considered placing orders for long lead time equipment under the Samsung Electro-Mechanics name first and then transferring the contracts to GlaSSEM.

A delay to Samsung Electro-Mechanics' glass substrate mass production timeline has likewise become unavoidable. Even if orders are placed within this year, factoring in equipment build times, the production line would be ready in the second half of next year at the earliest. The start of mass production is understood to have been pushed out to 2028 or later.

When GlaSSEM was established early last month, Samsung Electro-Mechanics presented a target of operations starting in the second half of 2027. At the recent second quarter earnings announcement, less than a month later, it revised the start of operations to 2028.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 12, 2026

>> Server DDR5 Memory Prices Rise 15% to 23% Across the Board This Month

• With memory makers continuing to raise prices through the third quarter, server DDR5 prices climbed 15% to 23% this month. Prices for 32GB, 64GB and 96GB DDR5 RDIMMs rose to $900, $1,590 and $2,650 respectively. On the spot market, they are trading at roughly $1,800 to $2,100, $3,000 to $3,200 and $3,800 to $4,100 respectively.

• Manufacturer DDR5 supply still falls short of demand, but as contract prices rise each quarter, large server customers are becoming more sensitive to the burden of memory costs.

• With long term supply agreements (LTAs) being signed one after another and large customers securing part of their DDR5 supply, the pace of DDR5 price increases is expected to gradually moderate.
